why_go: January brings peak Konkan winter—21-31C with dry skies. Sweet Lake's nightly drum circles run at full capacity, the main hippie gathering point. Beach time extends all day.
The driest month. 22-32C, water temperatures stable. Long-stay yoga residencies peak. Paragliding thermals are active. Beach traffic remains manageable.
Last cool window before April heat. 23-33C, still dry. Long-stay residencies wind down, freeing up accommodation. Hotel rates drop 20 percent.
Pre-monsoon heat arrives, though the main draw—Sweet Lake and drum circles—operates year-round. Beach time compresses to 6-9am and 5-9pm windows.
why_not: April heat peaks at 35C with 75 percent humidity, making daytime beach time uncomfortable and yoga schools closing.

why_go: May's peak heat is offset by dramatic pre-monsoon thunderstorms in weeks 3-4, which cool the air and attract a different crowd seeking the tempest.
why_not: Most beach shacks and restaurants close around May 31, humidity exceeds 80 percent, and water temperatures climb to body-heat levels.
Southwest monsoon arrives June 10 with 700-800mm rainfall. The beach becomes unusable, shacks dismantle, and water conditions are dangerous for swimming.
Peak monsoon with 900-1100mm rainfall. Beach closed entirely, shacks dismantled, and accommodation sparse. Skip entirely.
Monsoon continues with 500-700mm rainfall. Beach remains closed and the village enters full monsoon shutdown mode.

why_go: Monsoon retreats by month-end, allowing the first shacks to rebuild. Early signal of the return. 24-31C with lingering rain.
why_not: Monsoon rains remain frequent in early September, beaches stay muddy, and water remains unsafe for swimming. Shack rebuilding isn't complete.

why_go: Season officially opens October 1. 24-32C, monsoon spillover under 150mm. Shacks rebuilt, drum circles return mid-month. Gateway month to peak season.
Monsoon rains still linger into early October, keeping beaches choppy and some accommodation sparse.
Peak season builds steadily. 22-31C with rainfall under 30mm. Yoga residencies start, paragliding thermals active, drum circles nightly.
Peak season. 21-30C, completely dry. Christmas-NYE rates double, but drum circles run at full capacity and yoga schools are fully booked.
Peak Konkan window. 20-30C, dry. The restaurant village runs at full capacity—Gunpowder, Bomras, and Vinayak fish thali book 3-5 days in advance.
Driest month. 21-31C. Carnival parade reaches Mapusa five kilometres away. Restaurant village at peak. No other month matches the food-calendar concentration.
Last cool window. 22-32C. Restaurant booking lead times relax to 2-3 days. Hotel rates slide 15-20 percent, making long stays more affordable.
Pre-monsoon heat arrives but restaurants remain open. 24-34C, humidity 75 percent. Evening dining is still comfortable under AC.
why_not: Heat peaks at 34C with 75 percent humidity, making exploration between restaurants a sweat-soaked affair without AC.

why_go: Peak heat, but many restaurants adapt to shorter hours, shifting the rhythm to evening-only service. Pre-monsoon thunder weeks 3-4 offer drama and cooling.
why_not: Heat reaches 35C, humidity 80 percent. Most cafes reduce hours or close during peak afternoon, shrinking the dining window.

why_go: Southwest monsoon arrives with 700-800mm rain, but Assagao's inland location means less damage than the coast. Bomras and 2-3 others close, but the village functions.
why_not: Heavy monsoon rains force most cafes to close or drastically reduce hours, and exploring between venues requires rain gear and timing.
Peak monsoon with 900-1100mm rainfall. Most restaurant traffic collapses. Skip entirely.

why_go: Monsoon eases late-month. 24-29C, 500-700mm rain. Bomras reopens mid-August. The restaurant village rebuilds and begins operating again.
why_not: Heavy monsoon rains keep food and cafe scenes mostly closed throughout August, limiting dining options severely.

why_go: Monsoon retreats by mid-September. 24-31C, 250-300mm rain. Restaurant village fully open by month-end as beach Goa rebuilds inland.
Season opens. 23-31C, late-monsoon spillover under 150mm. Restaurant village at full rhythm. Anjuna shacks reopen October 1, driving visitor numbers up.
Peak builds. 21-30C, rainfall under 30mm. Saturday Night Market resumes. Restaurant booking lead times stretch to 2-4 days as crowds return.
Peak season. 20-30C, dry. Christmas-NYE rates double. Restaurant booking lead times extend to 7-10 days as the village hits capacity.
One of the better January windows for the Astavinayak pilgrimage. Crowds are moderate and weather supports temple walks across the eight sites.
February is one of the best months to traverse the circuit. Crowds, weather, and accessibility are all optimal across Morgaon, Siddhatek, Pali, Mahad, and beyond.
March remains a strong window. 22-32C. Crowds ease off after February. The circuit is fully accessible and weather supportive.
April is workable for the circuit. Crowds and weather are mid-range, though heat impacts the comfort of walking between temple sites.

why_not: May is a weaker window for the circuit. Heat, humidity, and unpredictable pre-monsoon storms make temple visits uncomfortable.

why_go: June is workable if you time visits for early mornings and handle occasional monsoon showers. The circuit remains accessible despite wet conditions.
why_not: June transitions to monsoon with unpredictable rainfall, making some temple access muddy and pilgrim numbers volatile.
July is a weaker window. Heavy monsoon rains make roads slick, temple approaches muddy, and pilgrim numbers drop sharply.

why_go: August is workable late-month as monsoon eases. Early August remains wet, but the latter half sees decreasing rainfall and path stabilization.
why_not: August monsoon rains make temple pathways muddy and crowd numbers remain low, reducing the pilgrim atmosphere.

why_go: September is workable. Crowds and weather normalize as monsoon retreats. The eight temples are fully accessible and pilgrim season resumes.
October is one of the better months. Early monsoon spillover clears quickly. The circuit is at full accessibility with good pilgrim energy.
November is one of the best months for the circuit. Weather and crowds are optimal. All eight temples are fully accessible with strong pilgrim foot traffic.
December remains strong. 21-28C, dry. All eight temples are fully accessible with healthy crowds. Year-end holidays drive pilgrim volumes up.
Post-monsoon flow remains strong. 20-32C. Falls run at 60 percent of peak monsoon discharge. Entry ₹50, 8am-6pm. Trails are dry and open.
why_not: Water volume drops sharply post-monsoon, so expect a fraction of the falls' full power compared to monsoon months.

why_go: Flow weakens but remains visible. 22-33C. Falls at 40 percent of monsoon peak. Trails are dry, weekday visits are quiet.
why_not: Water flow drops to annual lows as dry season intensifies, reducing the cascade to a moderately reduced stream.
Falls trickle by March. 24-35C. Flow drops to 20 percent of monsoon peak, making the visit less rewarding visually and physically.
Falls almost dry by April. 26-36C. Flow drops to 10 percent of monsoon peak as summer heat drains Kerala's cascades to a trickle.
Falls reduce to a trickle by May. 27-37C. Flow at 5-10 percent of peak as monsoon rains refuse to arrive.

why_go: Southwest monsoon begins June 1. 23-30C, 600-800mm rainfall. Falls rebuild to 60-80 percent of peak volume. Trail safety closures only on heaviest storm days.
Peak monsoon. 23-29C, 800-1000mm rainfall. Falls reach 90-100 percent of annual peak volume. Trail closures occur only on the wettest days.
Monsoon continues. 23-29C, 700-900mm rainfall. Falls hold at 90-95 percent of peak. Onam festival closes the town 3-4 days mid-month.
Monsoon retreats by month-end. 23-30C, 400-500mm rainfall easing. Falls maintain 80-90 percent of peak. Trails become more reliably open.
Optimal Athirapally window. 22-30C, 200-300mm rainfall. Falls hold at 80 percent of peak, trails fully open, weather settled. Peak season begins.
High-balance window. 21-30C, dry. Falls at 70 percent of peak. Trails fully open. Hotel rates climb 25 percent as demand peaks.
Peak Kerala season. 20-31C. Falls maintain 65 percent of monsoon peak volume. Christmas-NYE drives rates 2x and weekend gridlock.
why_not: Waterfall flow drops sharply post-monsoon, reducing volume to a fraction of what you see during monsoon months.

why_go: Peak Coromandel window. 20-30C, dry, northeast monsoon spent. Matrimandir meditation slots book 2-3 days out. Township farms at year-cleanest.
Driest month plus Auroville Marathon mid-February. 21-31C. Township beds tighten around marathon weekend. Meditation atmosphere peaks.
Last cool window. 24-33C, dry. Matrimandir slots open up as crowds ease post-March. Township room rates slide 15-20 percent.
Tamil Nadu plains heat arrives, but Matrimandir remains open. 28-38C, humidity 75 percent. April 24 darshan day closes township to visitors.
why_not: April heat peaks at 38C with negligible rainfall, making outdoor exploration of the ashram gardens uncomfortable.
Peak heat reaches 40C, humidity 80 percent. Outdoor township access collapses. The ashram grounds become nearly unbearable to explore.
Pre-monsoon heat plus early southwest monsoon squalls. 28-37C, humid, oppressive. Monsoon floods make June's humidity intolerable.

why_go: Mid-summer Coromandel humidity peaks. 27-35C, occasional storms, township somnolent. Monsoon rains flood the township and close most attractions.

why_not: Hot, sticky, and wet. 27-35C, humidity 85 percent. August 15 darshan plus Independence Day closures. Monsoon rains limit outdoor meditation.

why_go: Recovery month. 26-34C, humidity easing. Township returns to lighter schedules. Northeast monsoon arrives mid-October, so September is a transition month.
why_not: Monsoon rains persist into September, making it the township's wettest month with limited outdoor exploration.

why_go: Season opens but northeast monsoon arrives. 24-31C, 200-250mm rainfall. Matrimandir cycles slow on wet paths but meditation deepens.
why_not: Northeast monsoon arrives, making farm visits muddy and Matrimandir slots harder to secure due to weather closures.

why_go: Northeast monsoon tapers. 23-30C. November 24 darshan day mid-month. Township fully active. December peak-season rates kick in late-month.
Peak Coromandel month. 20-30C, dry, township at full capacity. Matrimandir slots tight during Christmas week but meditation community thrives.
Peak Chalukya window. 15-29C, dry. Cave 1-4 walks cleanest of the year. Agastya Lake reflections pristine. Cliff photography at year-best quality.
Driest month. 17-32C. Cliff-reflection photography at year-best. Day-trip axis to Aihole and Pattadakal cleanest. Airborne dust minimal.
Last cool month. 19-35C. Cave walks must compress before 11am as heat builds. Hotel rates ease 25 percent, accommodating budget trips.

why_not: Heat dome opens. 23-41C. Red sandstone cliffs radiate 48C+. The trip cannot happen mid-day. Cave interiors offer refuge but outdoor circuits become unsafe.
Heat peak. 25-43C. Cliff radiation exceeds 50C. Pre-monsoon dust storms obliterate visibility and make walking between caves dangerously hot.

why_go: Southwest monsoon light. 24-36C, 50-70mm rain. Heat eases considerably. Trip can happen in compressed windows if you plan around afternoon storms.
why_not: Monsoon floods make cave access unpredictable and roads occasionally impassable between sites.

why_go: Southwest monsoon active. 23-32C, 80-110mm rain. Agastya Lake fills. Walks viable in AM/PM windows with stone-dry interiors as refuge.
why_not: Monsoon rains make cave access treacherous and visibility poor for photographing rock-cut temple details.

why_go: Monsoon continues. 22-30C, 70-100mm rain. Tank fills completely. Green landscape emerging. Late-month offers off-peak pricing.
why_not: Monsoon flooding routinely submerges lower cave entrances and temple approaches, cutting access short.

why_go: Monsoon retreats. 21-29C, 50-70mm rain. Green-field landscape at peak beauty. Last off-peak window for affordable trips.
why_not: Monsoon humidity peaks while caves remain open, creating a comfort trade-off between stunning landscapes and muggy exploration.

why_go: Season opens. 19-30C, 30-50mm rain. Green-field landscape stunning. Cave walks return mid-month as ground dries. Airborne dust minimal.
Peak builds. 17-28C, dry. Karnataka Rajyotsava November 1. Cliff photography at year-cleanest air. Cave walks at peak comfort.
Peak season. 14-27C, dry. Christmas-NYE rates moderate. Cliffs at year-cleanest air. All four caves fully accessible.
Peak Bandipur access. 14-28C. Government safari ₹600-2500. Nilgiri Biosphere clear. Thick vegetation obscures some wildlife but cool temperatures favor activity.
why_not: Thick vegetation still obscures wildlife visibility, so expect sightings rather than guaranteed viewing.

why_go: Wildlife viewing peak opens. 15-30C. Tiger sighting odds jump to 1-in-20. Water concentration begins across the park, concentrating animals.
Peak wildlife window. 17-33C. Water shrinking accelerates animal congregation. Tiger sighting odds improve to 1-in-15.
Peak wildlife month. 20-35C. Sighting odds reach year-best 1-in-15. Pre-monsoon storms last 10 days but don't close the park.
Peak wildlife continues. 21-35C. First fortnight is peak. Last 10 days bring southwest monsoon advance but park remains open for safaris.
Southwest monsoon arrives. 19-27C, 150-250mm rainfall. Rain-shadow keeps rainfall lighter than Western Ghats. Park remains operational.
why_not: Monsoon rains close the park by mid-June, cutting your visit window short and sighting odds drop.

why_go: Southwest monsoon continues. 19-26C, 200-300mm rainfall. Some zones close but core park remains accessible. Sighting odds remain viable.
why_not: Monsoon rains keep many park zones closed, limiting safari routes and reducing your exploration area.

why_go: Southwest monsoon heaviest. 19-26C, 250-400mm rainfall. Many zones close but wait for October for full reopening.
why_not: Monsoon rainfall peaks, making multiple park zones inaccessible for safaris.

why_go: Southwest monsoon retreats. 18-27C, 150-250mm rainfall. Sighting odds begin easing as water becomes abundant again.
Season opens. 18-29C, 130-200mm rainfall. Northeast monsoon residual clears by month-end. Sighting odds climb as water shrinks again.
why_not: Thick monsoon vegetation limits wildlife visibility despite park reopening, so expect fewer sightings.

why_go: High season builds. 16-28C, dry. Sighting odds reach 1-in-20. Northeast monsoon residual eases completely.
why_not: Peak tiger-spotting hasn't fully arrived yet, so sightings remain unpredictable.

why_go: Peak season. 14-27C, dry. Christmas-NYE rates double. Sighting odds stable at 1-in-18. Year-cleanest visibility.
why_not: Peak tiger-spotting season hasn't fully arrived yet, so sightings remain less frequent than January-April.

why_go: Peak window. 24-29C, lagoon glassy, underwater viz 35m+. Bangaram Island Resort fully booked. The only legal-alcohol island in Lakshadweep.
Driest month. 24-30C. Manta ray sightings peak. Resort books 60 days in advance for Valentine through March. Dive conditions optimal.
Last cool window. 26-32C, dive viz 30m+. Resort shifts to shoulder pricing, 20-25 percent off February peak. Manta sightings remain frequent.
Pre-monsoon. 28-33C, humidity 80 percent. Lagoon remains calm. Heat dictates your schedule but the resort discounts 30 percent.
Late pre-monsoon. 28-33C. First half is viable but resort closes around May 10-15. Speedboat becomes unreliable last fortnight.
why_not: Pre-monsoon swells make water activities unpredictable, creating safety concerns for diving.
Southwest monsoon arrives. Resort closed. No access. 25-28C, 40-knot sustained winds, lagoon dangerous for boats.
Peak monsoon. Resort closed since May 15. No boat access. 350-450mm rainfall makes conditions unsafe.
Monsoon continues. Resort closed. 300-400mm rainfall. August 15 security tightening further restricts island access.

why_go: Resort reopens around September 25-30. Last week only is viable. 200-250mm rain mostly first half. Conditional on weather clearance.
Season opens. 100-150mm rain mostly first week. 25-31C. Resort at 70 percent capacity. Dive viz returns to 25m+.
why_not: Monsoon swells and rough seas make water activities unpredictable throughout the month.

why_go: Peak builds. 50-80mm rain. 23-30C. Manta sightings restart. Resort at 90 percent occupancy, books 45 days out.
Peak. 22-28C, dry, dive viz 32-35m. Christmas-NYE 50-60 percent premium. Resort 100 percent full. Manta sightings reliable.
Peak. 22-29C, dry. Convoy runs on schedule. Limestone caves and mud volcano fully operational. Requires 4am Port Blair start.
Driest, calmest month. 23-30C. Cave boat ride on glass-flat water. Convoy on strict schedule. Best month for the full experience.
Late peak. 25-31C. Cave entrance dry, mud volcano stable, mangrove creek boat calm. Day-trip prices 20 percent off February.
Hot 27-32C. Cave remains dry, creek boat calm, convoy runs on schedule. Big heat at the mud volcano but manageable early-morning starts.
why_not: April heat makes the 6-hour journey exhausting without adequate water and cooling stops.

why_go: Pre-monsoon first half is viable. Convoy and boat operations run early-month. After May 18 squalls begin increasing.
why_not: Pre-monsoon rains make the forest road impassable by regular vehicles by late May.
Monsoon arrives. ATR closes routinely for landslides. Creek boats cease operations. Cave access flooded.
Peak monsoon. ATR closed consistently. All headline activities cease. Skip entirely.
Monsoon continues. 460mm rainfall. ATR broken, boats off, cave flooded. Skip entirely.

why_go: Late monsoon. 320mm rain winding down. ATR repairs ongoing. Creek boats not yet running. Conditional on road clearance.
Recovery phase. 180mm rain mostly first week. ATR opens mid-month. Creek boats restart late-month. Last week becomes viable.
why_not: Monsoon rains make the sole forest road impassable for weeks, blocking access.

why_go: Properly open. 60mm rain, 23-30C. Convoy on schedule, creek boats daily, cave dry, mud volcano firm. Full experience accessible.
Peak. 22-29C, dry. Convoy reliable, cave dry, creek glass-flat. Christmas-NYE 40 percent premium. Full limestone-cave experience.
